lead: A virtual world is more than shapes. Each object needs rules that say what it does when a user grabs it, when a timer fires or when another object touches it. That is behavior modeling. The world also needs a database that stores every object, mesh, light, camera and panel in one searchable place. That is model management. Together they let a VR scene grow from a few test objects to a room, a building or a city without losing track of what exists and what should run.
prereq: You need: object shape and appearance and transformation hierarchies.

sections.h3: Behavior modeling: scripts, states and events

blocks.text: A behavior is a rule or set of rules attached to an object. It changes the object's attributes, plays feedback, or sends a message. The rule is stored in a script record: a small program with conditions and actions. A lamp script may check a switch attribute; when it is true, the script sets the light record on and plays a click sound. The script belongs to the object instance. It does not belong to each level of detail (LOD) mesh.

A state machine is a common way to write behavior. It lists states, such as closed, opening, open and closing for a door. An event, such as a hand press or a timer tick, triggers a transition only when its guard condition (a true/false test) is true. The transition runs an action. The door example: event press in state closed with guard unlocked → state opening; after 1 s timer → state open. Feedback is the visible, audible or haptic result: a door creak, a button colour change, a short vibration.

Events can come from input, collision, a timer or another script. Behavior runs in the world update loop: read events, test guards, change states, update attributes. The authoring tool stores the script with the object; playback runs it. Keep physics separate: physics computes forces in 4.3; behavior decides what to do with the result.

sections.h3: Model management: one database for the whole world

blocks.text: Model management is the scene database. It stores every record the world needs and gives each one an identity, a type and a place. World space is the common 3D coordinate frame for the whole scene. A point in world space is written (x, y, z) in metres, where x, y and z are distances along three axes. Each object also has a local transform: position and orientation relative to its parent. The hierarchy in 4.2 turns local transforms into world coordinates.

Record types include: geometry (tessellated data: vertices, triangles, normals, texture coordinates); appearance; LOD records (several mesh versions plus switch distances); bounding volume (a simple box or sphere around an object for fast tests); scripts and attributes (named values such as health, colour, speed); cullers and occluders (records that help discard unseen objects; selection is in 4.6); lights; cameras; 2D controls and control panels (buttons, sliders, labels); and room, stage or area descriptions (named regions with bounds).

Authoring writes these records; playback loads them, builds the hierarchy, starts scripts and draws frames. A culler is not the same as an occluder: a culler tests view volume, an occluder hides objects behind a large surface. A VR toolkit is only the container for the database; toolkit APIs and game engines are in Unit 5.

A managed world is counted by instances, not by rooms or by LODs. Let R be rooms, O objects per room, L LOD meshes per object, S scripts per object. The count starts from object instances and then multiplies by mesh or script records.
N<sub>obj</sub> = R × O; N<sub>mesh</sub> = N<sub>obj</sub> × L; N<sub>script</sub> = N<sub>obj</sub> × S
blocks.where: R is rooms; O is objects per room; L is LOD meshes per object; S is scripts per object; N<sub>obj</sub>, N<sub>mesh</sub> and N<sub>script</sub> are object, mesh and script record counts.

blocks.text: Use this when a question gives rooms, objects, LODs and scripts. The LOD count multiplies meshes only; it does not multiply scripts. A room with 50 objects and 3 LODs has 150 mesh records but 50 object records. If each object has 2 scripts, the room has 100 script records. Search and storage grow with the number of records, so model management needs names, types and bounds for queries.

World authoring and playback both use the same database. Authoring adds or edits records: a new chair, a changed script, a new light. Playback opens the database read-only, loads only needed rooms, and runs the update loop. A room description is a named area with bounds; it lets a query ask for 'all objects in room 2' without scanning the whole world. A control panel is a 2D record placed in the world; its buttons send events to scripts.

figure.caption: The count starts from object instances: 4 rooms × 50 objects = 200. Mesh records multiply by 3 LODs to 600, but script records multiply only by 2, giving 400.

spec.aria: Flow from 4 rooms and 50 objects per room to 200 object instances, then to 600 mesh records at 3 LODs each and 400 script records at 2 scripts each.

examples.question: A VR world has 4 rooms. Each room has 50 objects. Each object has 3 LOD meshes and 2 scripts. Count the object instances, the mesh records and the script records.
steps: Rooms R = 4; objects per room O = 50.
Object instances N<sub>obj</sub> = R × O = 4 × 50 = 200 objects.
Each object has L = 3 LOD mesh records. Mesh records N<sub>mesh</sub> = 200 × 3 = 600 mesh records.
Each object has S = 2 script records. Script records N<sub>script</sub> = 200 × 2 = 400 script records.
examples.answer: The world has 200 object instances, 600 mesh records and 400 script records.
examples.check:
rooms = 4
objects_per_room = 50
lods = 3
scripts = 2
objects = rooms * objects_per_room
mesh_records = objects * lods
script_records = objects * scripts
print(objects)
print(mesh_records)
print(script_records)

traps: A script attaches to an object instance, not to each LOD. A 3-LOD object still has one record per script, not three.
World space is one common frame; local position is relative to a parent. Do not add parent and child positions as if both were already world coordinates.
Model management stores records. Rendering, culling choice and LOD switching are separate stages; see 4.5 and 4.6.
A state is not a transition. 'Door open' is a state; 'press closes it' is an event that triggers a transition.
A bounding volume is a cheap approximation, not the visible mesh. It may be larger than the object.

quiz.a: A program stored with an object that runs conditions and actions on events or updates.

quiz.q: Why does a script not multiply with LOD count?
quiz.a: A script controls the object instance; LOD records only swap meshes for that same instance.

quiz.q: A world has 3 rooms, 40 objects per room, 2 LODs per object, 4 scripts per object. Find object, mesh and script records.
A door opens visually but no creak plays. Which records do you inspect and why?
quiz.a: Inspect the door's script or state machine and its audio feedback record. The state may change without running the action, or the sound record may be missing or disabled.
The common 3D coordinate frame for the whole scene, with positions in metres.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a culler and an occluder?
quiz.a: A culler rejects records outside the view; an occluder hides objects behind a large surface. Both reduce drawing, by different tests.

quiz.q: A room has 25 objects, each with 3 LODs. A script is attached to every object. Count mesh and script records if each object has 1 script.
When is a bounding volume useful in model management?
quiz.a: For fast culling, collision broad phase and spatial queries. It is not the visible mesh and can be conservative.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production VR databases often separate asset data (shared meshes) from scene instances (placed objects), so 200 chairs share one mesh but keep 200 transforms. Entity-component-system (ECS) designs push behavior into small components and systems. World partition and streaming load rooms on demand. Search terms: scene database, entity component system, behavior tree, state machine, occlusion culling, world partition.
